theorems.name: Corollary 5 (of Theorem~ \ref{t_modif1})
theorems.body: For any vertices $i,j\in V$ such that $i\ne j,$\begin{eqnarray*}  d^{\hspace{.04em}{\rm \scriptscriptstyle L}e\hspace{-.05em}{\rm \scriptscriptstyle W}}(i,j) =\frac{\theta _\infty }{2\rho }\, (\widetilde c^{\, i(j)}+\widetilde c^{\hspace{.07em}j(i)}). \end{eqnarray*}
theorems.slogan: The effective resistance between two distinct vertices i and j in a graph equals a constant factor times the sum of two commute times. The constant factor is theta infinity divided by two times rho. The commute times are from i to j and from j to i. This formula relates graph distances to random walk properties.

theorems.name: Theorem 2.2 (\cite {CRRST97})
theorems.body: For any pair of vertices $u,v \in V$, $ \mathsf{C}(u,v) = 2 |E| \cdot \mathsf{R}(u,v). $
theorems.slogan: The effective resistance between any two vertices in a graph equals the commute time between them divided by twice the number of edges.

theorems.name: Proposition 2.4 ({\bf Commute-Time Identity}, Corollary 2.21 in \cite{LP})
theorems.body: Let $G$ be a finite connected network and let $a$ and $z$ be two vertices of $G$. The commute time between $a$ and $z$ is\[  \mathbb {E}_a\left[H_z\right]+\mathbb {E}_z\left[H_a\right]= \mathcal{R}(a\leftrightarrow z)\times \left(\sum _{x\in V}\pi (x)\right).  \]
theorems.slogan: The commute time between two vertices in a finite connected network equals the effective resistance between them multiplied by the sum of the stationary probabilities over all vertices.
